analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give workers paid rest, restroom, medical breaks and meal periods.
analysis.headline: A federal bill requiring meal, rest, and restroom breaks for hourly workers was introduced in June 2024 with 37 Democratic cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law today requires employers to pay workers for time worked and to give nursing mothers pumping breaks, but sets no general minimum for meal, rest, or bathroom breaks. This bill would have added those guarantees to the Fair Labor Standards Act: a 30-minute meal break per six hours worked, at least a 10-minute paid break every four hours, and short paid medical breaks as needed. Workers who are not fully relieved of duties during a meal break would be paid for it at time-and-a-half, and employers could not force workers to skip breaks. States and union contracts offering stronger protections would be untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers, especially in jobs like fast food, warehousing, retail, and call centers where workers commonly work six-hour-plus stretches with no guaranteed break, and where bathroom access can be tightly restricted. Workers who must stay on-site or stay reachable during a meal break would now be paid for it at 1.5 times their regular rate. Workers needing short medical breaks would get paid time for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers with no guaranteed breaks

how_it_helps.text: Requires a 30-minute meal break during every six-hour work period, and a break of at least 10 minutes (or enough time to reach a working restroom) every four hours [S2].

Pays workers at time-and-a-half for any meal break during which they are not fully relieved of work or free to leave the work site, and pays for all rest and medical breaks at their regular rate [S2].
Prohibits employers from pressuring workers to waive their meal break, and makes violations enforceable under the Fair Labor Standards Act with the same legal remedies as wage violations [S2].
Leaves stronger state laws and collective bargaining agreements in place, so no worker could be moved backward to weaker protections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, particularly labor-intensive service and logistics businesses, would face the cost of covering work during guaranteed breaks, paying for breaks where workers are not fully relieved, and potential lawsuits and penalties for violations.

drawbacks.text: The default meal break is unpaid, so a worker who takes the break and goes without pay for 30 minutes still loses earnings under the bill's baseline [S2].

Employers would bear real costs: they must staff or pay for work covered during guaranteed breaks, pay time-and-a-half when workers remain on duty, and face legal liability for violations under the FLSA's penalty structure [S2].

The bill allows workers to waive their meal break by consent, and while it forbids employers from compelling a waiver, relying on worker 'consent' can be hard to police where workers fear retaliation [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a first-ever federal guarantee of the most basic breaks—time to eat, use the bathroom, and manage a medical condition—paid when the worker is not truly free. The costs fall on employers, who would pass some of them into prices or scheduling, and the bill leaves the meal break itself unpaid by default, which a stronger version might have changed. The waiver-by-consent provision is a weak point. On balance it is a clear gain for workers, with the burden shifted to their employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee when introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it never reached a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the Worker Rights and Support Act on June 28, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S4].
Thirty-seven House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did [S3].
No further action was recorded—no committee markup, no hearing, no floor vote—and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of hourly workers are better off: they continue operating without any federal obligation to provide or pay for breaks, and avoided the compliance costs and liability the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 37 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup, hearing, or vote during the rest of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action.

industries.industry: Hourly-wage employers (fast food, retail, warehousing, call centers)
industries.note: These employers would have to build guaranteed, and in some cases paid, break time into their schedules and could face lawsuits for violations. Their interest in avoiding those requirements runs against workers' interest in break time, since the bill's whole purpose is to stop these industries from keeping workers on the clock without relief.

The bill does not override collective bargaining agreements, so union contracts with existing break provisions would stay in force; nothing weaker could replace them. Workers under those contracts keep whatever they already bargained for.
